strengths.title: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation
strengths.description: The symmetric collaborative dialogue setting is genuinely underexplored and occupies a conceptually novel space between task-oriented and open-domain dialogue. The motivation is clear: agents with private knowledge must communicate strategically using both structured knowledge and open-ended language. This bridges two important dialogue paradigms.
evidence: Introduction (lines 001–050) clearly articulates the gap between task-oriented systems (fixed slots) and open-domain systems (no structured state)
Figure 1 example effectively demonstrates conversational implicature that cannot be captured by slot-value pairs
Table 1 shows diverse semantics ('most of', 'might be') that resist traditional state representation
Section 2.1 formalizes the task clearly and notes parallels to human-computer collaboration with different expertise

strengths.title: Substantial and efficiently collected human-human dialogue corpus
strengths.description: The dataset contribution is significant: 11K human-human dialogues collected in 13.5 hours on AMT, with 79% success rate. The corpus exhibits documented linguistic and strategic phenomena (coreference, cross-talk, external knowledge use, strategic entity/attribute ordering) that are well-analyzed and reported.
evidence: Section 2.2: 11,439 dialogues collected in 13.5 hours (efficient crowdsourcing)
Table 3: 9,041 completed dialogues with detailed statistics (vocabulary size, utterance length, linguistic templates)
Section 2.3: Comprehensive documentation of linguistic phenomena (Table 2) including coreference, cross-talk (30% of utterances), external knowledge use
Section 2.3: Strategic behavior analysis showing human preference for low-cardinality attributes first (footnote 5)
Appendix H: Example dialogues showing linguistic diversity and strategic behavior

strengths.title: Methodologically innovative dual evaluation framework
strengths.description: The paper proposes and implements a thoughtful dual evaluation methodology (partner + third-party) that reveals different aspects of dialogue quality. Partner evaluation captures task success and coherence; third-party evaluation captures informality and linguistic markers. The discrepancy analysis (lines 668–698) provides valuable insights into evaluation mode differences.
evidence: Section 4.2 (Partner Evaluation, lines 606–640): Interactive evaluation where humans rate their conversational partners on fluency, correctness, cooperation, human-likeness
Section 4.2 (Third-party Evaluation, lines 656–698): External observer evaluation with access to one agent's KB
Lines 668–698: Qualitative analysis of discrepancies between evaluation modes, noting different standards and what each mode captures
Table 5: Ratings from both evaluation modes showing systematic differences (e.g., DynoNet cooperation: 4.0 partner vs 3.8 third-party)

strengths.title: Comprehensive documentation of linguistic and pragmatic phenomena
strengths.description: The paper thoroughly documents complex linguistic phenomena in collaborative dialogue (coreference, conjunctions, cross-talk, external knowledge use, multi-type/multi-entity utterances) with quantitative statistics and qualitative examples. This contributes to understanding dialogue complexity beyond slot-value representations.
evidence: Table 2: Systematic categorization of linguistic phenomena with examples (coreference, conjunctions, cross-talk, external knowledge, self-correction, chit-chat)
Section 2.3: Quantitative statistics (7.4% multi-type utterances, 30.9% multi-entity utterances, 30% cross-talk)
Table 1: Example utterances showing diverse semantics and pragmatic phenomena
Table 6: Example dialogues showing linguistic diversity and strategic behavior
Appendix H: Additional example dialogues demonstrating phenomena

strengths.title: Clear architectural design integrating structured and unstructured representations
strengths.description: DynoNet's architecture is well-motivated and clearly described. The combination of knowledge graphs (structured) with recurrent neural embeddings (unstructured) is a reasonable approach to modeling dialogue state that requires both grounding and flexibility. The three components (dynamic knowledge graph, graph embedding, utterance generation) are well-articulated.
evidence: Section 3 provides clear overview of three components: dynamic knowledge graph, graph embedding, utterance generation
Section 3.1: Knowledge graph construction is clearly explained with example (Figure 2)
Section 3.2: Graph embedding mechanism is well-motivated (combining structural properties, mention vectors, recursive node embeddings)
Section 3.3: Utterance generation with attention mechanism and copying is clearly described
Section 3.4: Entity abstraction design is well-motivated (context-dependent rather than lookup-table embeddings)

concerns.title: Critical contradiction: Task success claim contradicted by empirical results
concerns.description: The paper claims DynoNet 'outperforms baselines' but Table 4 shows DynoNet underperforms Rule baseline on primary task success metrics: CT (0.80 vs 0.82 per turn), CS (0.89 vs 0.91 per selection). This is a fundamental inconsistency between the main claim and the data.
evidence: Table 4: DynoNet CT=0.80, Rule CT=0.82 (DynoNet underperforms by 0.02)
Table 4: DynoNet CS=0.89, Rule CS=0.91 (DynoNet underperforms by 0.02)
Abstract: Claims 'more effective at achieving the goal' but data contradicts this
Introduction (lines 020–025): Positions DynoNet as superior but task success metrics show otherwise
Section 4.2 (lines 573–580): Discusses strategy matching but does not acknowledge task success underperformance
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Revise claims to accurately reflect empirical results. Either: (1) acknowledge that DynoNet underperforms Rule on task success but excels on human-likeness ratings, or (2) provide analysis of why task success is not the primary metric of interest. Clarify what 'outperformance' means in context of mixed results.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing for any performance comparisons
concerns.description: The paper reports performance metrics (loss, task success, human ratings) without statistical significance testing. Differences of 0.02 in task success rate or 0.3–0.5 points on 5-point rating scales may not be meaningful without significance tests. This undermines confidence in claimed improvements.
evidence: Table 4: Loss differences (2.16 vs 2.20 vs 2.26) reported without significance tests
Table 4: Task success differences (0.80 vs 0.82 vs 0.91) reported without significance tests
Table 5: Human rating differences (e.g., cooperation 4.0 vs 3.5 vs 2.8) reported without significance tests or confidence intervals
Table 7: Ablation study loss differences (0.05–0.10 points) reported without significance tests
Section 4.2 and 4.3: No mention of statistical testing methodology or p-values
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance testing (e.g., t-tests, ANOVA) for all performance comparisons. Report p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes. For human ratings, report inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa) and sample sizes per condition.

concerns.title: Ablation study incomplete: only dev set loss, no task-level validation
concerns.description: Table 7 shows ablation study results using only dev set cross-entropy loss. No evaluation of architectural components on task success rate or human ratings. This makes it impossible to assess whether loss improvements translate to practical benefits or whether components are truly 'critical'.
evidence: Table 7: Ablation study reports only dev set loss (ℓ) for K ∈ {0,1,2} and entity abstraction
Section 4.3 (lines 707–715): No mention of task success or human evaluation for ablated models
Discussion (line 775): Claims message passing is 'crucial' but ablation shows only 0.10-point loss improvement (2.16 vs 2.26)
No analysis of which components contribute to which aspects of performance (strategy learning, human-likeness, task success)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Extend ablation study to include: (1) task success rate (CT, CS) for each ablated model, (2) human evaluation (partner and third-party ratings) for at least K=0 and K=2 variants, (3) strategy metrics (#Ent1, |Attr1|) to assess whether message passing improves strategy learning. This will clarify whether components are truly critical for task performance.

concerns.title: Human-likeness ratings lack inter-rater reliability and statistical validation
concerns.description: Partner and third-party evaluations report human-likeness ratings (1–5 scale) without inter-rater reliability metrics (Krippendorff's alpha, Cohen's kappa) or statistical significance testing. Discrepancies between evaluation modes (lines 668–698) suggest ratings measure different constructs, but this is not quantified.
evidence: Table 5: Human-likeness ratings reported (e.g., DynoNet 3.8 partner, 3.5 third-party) without confidence intervals or significance tests
Section 4.2 (lines 606–640): Partner evaluation methodology described but no inter-rater reliability reported
Section 4.2 (lines 656–698): Third-party evaluation methodology described but no inter-rater reliability reported
Footnote 15: 'At least 5 people' per agent but total sample size N not specified; unclear if this is sufficient for reliable ratings
Lines 668–698: Qualitative analysis of discrepancies but no quantitative correlation analysis between evaluation modes
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-rater reliability metrics (Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa) for both partner and third-party evaluations. Conduct statistical significance testing (e.g., t-tests) for rating differences. Quantify correlation between partner and third-party ratings to assess whether they measure different constructs. Report sample sizes (N) for each evaluation condition.

concerns.title: Training only on successful dialogues introduces selection bias
concerns.description: Section 4.1 states 'only train on successful dialogues' (79% of dataset). This introduces selection bias: models may overfit to successful dialogue patterns and fail to learn recovery strategies or error handling. No analysis of failed dialogues or comparison of training on all vs. successful dialogues only.
evidence: Section 4.1 (line 510): 'only train on successful dialogues'
Table 3: 9,041 completed dialogues out of 11,439 (79% success rate); 21% of data excluded from training
Section 2.2: No analysis of failed dialogues or their characteristics
No comparison of model performance when trained on all vs. successful dialogues only
No discussion of how this affects generalization to test set (which may include failed dialogues)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze characteristics of failed dialogues (21% of dataset). Train models on both successful and all dialogues and compare performance. Report whether test set includes failed dialogues and how model performance differs on successful vs. failed test cases. Discuss implications for generalization.

concerns.title: Entity linking accuracy not evaluated; potential bottleneck unquantified
concerns.description: Section 3.1 mentions 'rule-based lexicon to link text spans to entities' (Appendix D) but provides no evaluation of entity linking accuracy. Errors in entity linking could corrupt node embeddings and dialogue state representation, but this potential bottleneck is not analyzed.
evidence: Section 3.1 (line 309): 'We use a rule-based lexicon to link text spans to entities. See details in Appendix D.'
No evaluation of entity linking accuracy reported in main text or appendix
No analysis of error propagation when entity linking fails
Table 6 example shows DynoNet 'lying' (claiming false information); unclear if this is due to entity linking errors or model generation errors
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate entity linking accuracy on a sample of test dialogues (e.g., 100 dialogues). Report precision, recall, and F1 score. Analyze error propagation: how do entity linking errors affect downstream model performance (task success, human ratings)? Discuss whether entity linking is a bottleneck limiting model performance.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing under 5-minute time pressure may not reflect natural dialogue
concerns.description: Section 2.2 states 'randomly pairing up users to perform the task within 5 minutes'. Time pressure may introduce artifacts (abbreviated language, rushed strategies) not representative of natural dialogue. No analysis of how time pressure affects dialogue quality, strategy, or linguistic naturalness.
evidence: Section 2.2 (line 220): 'within 5 minutes'
Section 2.2 (line 221): 'prevent users from selecting more than once every 10 seconds' (additional time pressure)
No analysis of dialogue characteristics under time pressure vs. unconstrained dialogue
No comparison of linguistic naturalness or strategic behavior to other dialogue corpora
Section 2.3 documents linguistic phenomena but does not discuss whether time pressure affects their frequency or naturalness
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze impact of time pressure on dialogue characteristics. Compare linguistic features (utterance length, vocabulary diversity, dialogue acts) to other dialogue corpora. Conduct analysis of whether models trained on time-pressured dialogue generalize to unconstrained dialogue. Consider collecting a small sample of unconstrained dialogues for comparison.

concerns.title: Only one domain evaluated; generalization claims unsupported
concerns.description: The paper evaluates only the MutualFriends domain. No cross-domain evaluation or analysis of generalization to other collaborative tasks with different knowledge structures, communication goals, or strategic considerations. Claims about the task's importance and broad applicability are unsupported.
evidence: Section 2.1: Task defined for MutualFriends domain (friends with attributes like school, company, hobby)
Section 2.2: 'We created a schema containing 7 attributes and more than 3K entities' (domain-specific)
No mention of other domains or cross-domain evaluation

Discussion (lines 725–750): Claims the setting 'has parallels in human-computer collaboration' and is 'a good stepping stone towards learning more complex dialogues such as negotiation' but provides no evidence
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate DynoNet on at least one additional domain (e.g., product recommendation, travel planning, or negotiation). Analyze whether architectural components (message passing, entity abstraction) generalize across domains. Discuss domain-specific vs. domain-general aspects of the approach.

concerns.title: Foundational assumption: utterance-level likelihood maximization may be insufficient
concerns.description: Section 4.1 states 'maximize the likelihood of each utterance from perspectives of both agents'. This utterance-level objective may not be sufficient for task-oriented dialogue. No comparison to task-level reward signals (e.g., reinforcement learning). Task success rates below human performance (Table 4: DynoNet 0.80 vs Humans 0.95) suggest this assumption may be violated.
evidence: Section 4.1 (lines 501–510): 'maximize the likelihood of each utterance from perspectives of both agents'
No reinforcement learning or task-level reward signal
No analysis of whether utterance-level loss correlates with task success
Table 4: Substantial gap between DynoNet (0.80 per turn) and human performance (0.95 per turn)
No comparison to models trained with task-level objectives
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze correlation between test loss and task success rate. Compare utterance-level likelihood maximization to task-level reward signals (e.g., reinforcement learning with task success as reward). Discuss whether utterance-level training is sufficient for task-oriented dialogue or whether task-level objectives are necessary.

concerns.title: Loss as proxy for dialogue quality: no validation against downstream metrics
concerns.description: Table 4 reports test cross-entropy loss as primary automatic metric, but no correlation analysis between test loss and task success rate or human ratings. Architectural improvements that reduce loss may not improve task success or human satisfaction.
evidence: Table 4: Test loss (ℓ) reported as primary automatic metric
No correlation analysis between test loss and task success (CT, CS) or human ratings
Loss improvements (DynoNet 2.16 vs StanoNet 2.20) are modest and not validated against downstream metrics
Section 4.2: Automatic evaluation section reports loss but does not discuss its relationship to task success or human evaluation
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute correlation coefficients (Pearson or Spearman) between test loss and task success rate, and between test loss and human ratings. Discuss whether loss is a valid proxy for dialogue quality. If correlation is weak, consider alternative automatic metrics or emphasize human evaluation results.

concerns.title: Example dialogue shows model 'lying' but impact on evaluation unclear
concerns.description: Table 6 shows DynoNet claiming 'a morning friend who likes outdoor' when this is false (not in its KB). This suggests the model generates hallucinated information. Impact on task success and human evaluation is unclear; partner evaluation may miss such errors if task succeeds.
evidence: Table 6: DynoNet utterance 'I have a morning friend who likes outdoor' when this is not in its KB
Section 4.2 (lines 606–640): Partner evaluation notes DynoNet 'cooperates smoothly' and receives high cooperation rating (4.0) despite lying
No analysis of hallucination frequency or impact on task success
No discussion of whether partner evaluation can detect such errors
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze frequency of hallucinated information in model outputs. Evaluate whether partner evaluators can detect hallucinations. Discuss implications for task success and human satisfaction. Consider adding explicit correctness checks to evaluation.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter tuning on dev set without analysis of dev/test similarity
concerns.description: Section 4.1 states 'Hyperparameters are tuned on the dev set' but provides no analysis of dev/test set similarity or performance gap. Potential for overfitting to dev set characteristics; reported improvements may be artifacts of dev set tuning.
evidence: Section 4.1 (line 510): 'Hyperparameters are tuned on the dev set'
No analysis of dev/test set similarity or performance gap
Ablation study (Table 7) uses dev set loss only
No discussion of whether hyperparameters optimized for dev set generalize to test set
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report dev/test set performance gap for baseline models. Analyze whether dev and test sets have similar characteristics (e.g., dialogue length, entity/attribute distributions). Consider using cross-validation or held-out validation set for hyperparameter tuning.

concerns.title: Limited novelty of architectural components
concerns.description: DynoNet combines existing ideas (graph embeddings, recurrent memory updates, attention mechanisms) into a coherent system for a specific task. Message passing over knowledge graphs is a natural extension of EntNet and graph neural networks, not a conceptual leap. The architectural novelty is incremental.
evidence: Section 3.2: Message passing mechanism is similar to belief propagation and graph neural networks
Discussion (line 775): 'Our network architecture is most similar to EntNet (Henaff et al., 2017), where memories are also updated by input sentences recurrently'
Section 3.4: Entity abstraction is a design choice but not a novel concept
Ablation study (Table 7) shows modest improvements from message passing (0.10-point loss improvement)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the novelty of architectural components relative to EntNet and graph neural networks. Emphasize the problem formulation and dataset contribution as primary novelties rather than architectural innovation.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly comparable architecture for dialogue state representation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: DynoNet extends EntNet by structuring entities as a knowledge graph and propagating information via message passing. EntNet uses unstructured memory updates; DynoNet adds graph structure. The paper acknowledges this similarity (Discussion, line 775) but claims message passing is 'crucial' (line 775)—a claim weakly supported by ablation study (0.10-point loss improvement).
comparable_works.source_trace: Discussion (line 775): 'Our network architecture is most similar to EntNet (Henaff et al., 2017)'

comparable_works.relevance: Alternative approach to dialogue state representation without domain-specific features
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Bordes & Weston (2017) propose Memory Networks without domain-specific features. DynoNet differs by embedding both dialogue history and KB structurally (via knowledge graphs) rather than relying on unstructured memory and API calls. The paper positions DynoNet as more structured than Memory Networks.
comparable_works.source_trace: Discussion (lines 745–755): 'However, the memory is unstructured and interfacing with KBs relies on API calls, whereas our model embeds both the dialogue history and the KB structurally.'

comparable_works.citation_label: POMDP-based dialogue systems (Young et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2017)
comparable_works.relevance: Traditional task-oriented dialogue systems with handcrafted dialogue states
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: POMDP-based systems require handcrafted slots and dialogue acts, limiting scalability. DynoNet aims to learn dialogue state representation automatically. However, DynoNet's task success rates (0.80 per turn) are comparable to or worse than rule-based baselines (0.82 per turn), suggesting POMDP-based approaches may still be competitive.
comparable_works.source_trace: Discussion (lines 725–745): 'Most task-oriented dialogue systems follow the POMDP-based approach (Young et al., 2013). Despite their success (Wen et al., 2017; Dhingra et al., 2016), the requirement for handcrafted slots limits their scalability...'

comparable_works.citation_label: Dialogue State Tracking Challenge (Williams et al., 2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Benchmark for dialogue state representation in task-oriented systems
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: DSTC focuses on slot-value state tracking in information-seeking dialogues. The symmetric collaborative dialogue task is more complex (private knowledge, strategic communication) and requires richer state representation. However, the paper does not compare to DSTC baselines or datasets.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature: 'The Dialog State Tracking Challenge Series' (Williams et al., 2016)

comparable_works.citation_label: Open-domain dialogue systems (Shang et al., 2015; Serban et al., 2015b; Li et al., 2016a)
comparable_works.relevance: Alternative paradigm for dialogue without structured state
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Open-domain systems learn direct mappings from utterances to next utterance without structured state. DynoNet combines structured knowledge with open-ended dialogue, positioning itself as a middle ground. However, the paper does not compare to open-domain baselines.
comparable_works.source_trace: Introduction (lines 010–020): 'In contrast, recent open-domain chat systems (Shang et al., 2015; Serban et al., 2015b; Sordoni et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016a) learn a mapping directly from previous utterances to the next utterance.'

uncertainty_flags: CRITICAL: Task success rates contradict main claim of outperformance. DynoNet (0.80 per turn, 0.89 per selection) underperforms Rule baseline (0.82 per turn, 0.91 per selection). This is a fundamental inconsistency between claims and data.

Human-likeness ratings are subjective and lack inter-rater reliability metrics. Discrepancies between partner and third-party evaluators (lines 668–698) suggest ratings measure different constructs, but this is not quantified.

No statistical significance testing reported for any performance comparisons (loss, task success, human ratings). Differences of 0.02 in task success or 0.3–0.5 points on 5-point scales may not be meaningful.
Ablation study uses only dev set loss; no evaluation on task success or human ratings. Impossible to assess whether loss improvements translate to practical benefits.
Entity linking accuracy not evaluated; potential source of error propagation through model. Rule-based lexicon (Appendix D) may be a bottleneck.
Only one domain (MutualFriends) evaluated; generalization to other collaborative tasks unclear. Claims about task importance and broad applicability are unsupported.
Training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset) introduces selection bias. No analysis of failed dialogues or comparison of training on all vs. successful dialogues only.
Crowdsourcing under 5-minute time pressure may not reflect natural dialogue. No analysis of time pressure effects on dialogue quality or strategy.
Partner evaluation ratings may be confounded by task success or dialogue length. No correlation analysis between ratings and confounding variables.
Third-party evaluators cannot assess correctness reliably (acknowledged: 'judgment on correctness is a mere guess', lines 668–673). Reliability of third-party ratings questionable.
Modest improvements in test loss (0.05–0.10 points) between DynoNet and baselines. Practical significance unclear without significance tests.
No analysis of which architectural components (message passing vs. entity abstraction) contribute to which aspects of performance (strategy learning, human-likeness, task success).
Example dialogue (Table 6) shows DynoNet 'lying' (claiming false information). Impact on task success and human evaluation unclear.
Hyperparameter tuning on dev set without analysis of dev/test similarity. Potential for overfitting; reported improvements may be artifacts of dev set tuning.
No comparison of utterance-level likelihood maximization to task-level reward signals (e.g., reinforcement learning). Foundational assumption unvalidated.
Substantial gap between DynoNet (0.80–0.89) and human performance (0.95–0.98) on task success suggests architectural limitations not discussed.
alternative_interpretations: Task success metrics (Table 4) could be interpreted as evidence that Rule baseline is more effective than DynoNet for task completion, contradicting the main claim. The paper's focus on human-likeness ratings may reflect an implicit shift in evaluation priorities away from task success.

The discrepancy between partner and third-party evaluation (lines 668–698) could indicate that partner evaluators are biased by task success (if the dialogue succeeds, they rate the partner highly regardless of quality), while third-party evaluators apply more objective standards. This would suggest partner evaluation is less reliable than third-party evaluation.

Strategy learning (Table 4: #Ent1, |Attr1|) could be an artifact of the data distribution rather than learned behavior. StanoNet (0.67) nearly matches DynoNet (0.68) on #Ent1, suggesting strategy learning may not require message passing. The paper does not analyze whether models generalize to different KB distributions.

The 'lying' example (Table 6) could indicate that the model prioritizes fluency and cooperation over correctness. Partner evaluation may reward this behavior (high cooperation rating despite false information), suggesting partner evaluation is not a reliable measure of dialogue quality.

The modest loss improvements from message passing (0.05–0.10 points, Table 7) could be within noise or due to overfitting to dev set. Without significance tests, it is unclear whether message passing provides meaningful benefits.

The 79% success rate in crowdsourcing could indicate that the task is too difficult or the interface is confusing, rather than reflecting natural dialogue difficulty. This could affect the representativeness of the dataset.
The 5-minute time pressure could be a feature rather than a limitation, if the goal is to study dialogue under realistic time constraints. However, the paper does not discuss this trade-off.
transparency_notes: This review identifies a critical inconsistency between the paper's main claim (DynoNet outperforms baselines) and empirical evidence (task success rates show DynoNet underperforms Rule). This is not a matter of interpretation but a factual contradiction in the data.

The paper's strongest evidence for DynoNet superiority comes from human-likeness ratings, which are subjective and lack statistical validation. The discrepancy between partner and third-party evaluation suggests these ratings measure different constructs, but this is not quantified.

Multiple methodological concerns (no significance testing, incomplete ablation study, selection bias from training on successful dialogues only, entity linking accuracy not evaluated) reduce confidence in the empirical results. These are not minor issues but fundamental aspects of experimental rigor.

The dataset contribution is substantial and well-documented. The dual evaluation framework is methodologically innovative. However, these strengths do not offset the weaknesses in empirical validation of the main claims.
The paper's focus on human-likeness ratings rather than task success may reflect an implicit shift in evaluation priorities. This should be made explicit and justified.
The claim that message passing is 'crucial' (Discussion, line 775) is not well-supported by the ablation study, which shows only a 0.10-point loss improvement. This is an overstatement.

The paper does not discuss the substantial gap between DynoNet (0.80 per turn) and human performance (0.95 per turn) on task success. This gap suggests architectural limitations that deserve analysis.
The paper's generalization claims (e.g., 'a good stepping stone towards learning more complex dialogues such as negotiation') are unsupported by evidence. Only one domain is evaluated.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The problem formulation (symmetric collaborative dialogue) is genuinely novel and underexplored. However, the architectural innovation (DynoNet) is incremental over EntNet and graph neural networks. The dataset contribution is substantial but limited to one domain. The novelty is primarily in problem formulation and dataset, not in architectural design.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If task success rates showed DynoNet outperforming Rule (e.g., 0.85 vs 0.82 per turn), the main claim would be supported by empirical evidence.
If human-likeness ratings were validated with inter-rater reliability metrics and statistical significance testing, the evidence for DynoNet superiority would be stronger.
If the ablation study included task success and human evaluation metrics (not just dev set loss), the claim that message passing is 'critical' would be better supported.
If the paper evaluated DynoNet on multiple domains (not just MutualFriends), generalization claims would be credible.
If the paper compared utterance-level likelihood maximization to task-level reward signals (e.g., reinforcement learning), the foundational assumption would be validated.
If entity linking accuracy were evaluated and shown to be high (>95%), the potential bottleneck would be ruled out.

If the paper analyzed the impact of time pressure on dialogue characteristics and showed that models trained on time-pressured dialogue generalize to unconstrained dialogue, the dataset's representativeness would be established.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes meaningful contributions to problem formulation, dataset creation, and evaluation methodology. However, critical inconsistencies between claims and empirical evidence, combined with methodological concerns (no significance testing, incomplete ablation study, selection bias, entity linking not evaluated), reduce confidence in the main claims. The task success metrics directly contradict the claim of outperformance, which is a fundamental issue. The dataset contribution is substantial and the dual evaluation framework is innovative, which supports the upper bound. However, the architectural novelty is incremental and the empirical validation is weak, which supports the lower bound. Overall confidence is moderate, reflecting the mixed quality of the work.

consensus_findings: The paper makes substantial contributions in problem formulation (symmetric collaborative dialogue task) and dataset creation (11K human-human dialogues with documented linguistic phenomena), which are widely recognized as valuable by all reviewers.

A critical contradiction exists between the main claim (DynoNet outperforms baselines) and empirical evidence: task success metrics show DynoNet underperforms Rule baseline (0.80 vs 0.82 per turn; 0.89 vs 0.91 per selection). All reviewers identify this as a major inconsistency.

Human-likeness ratings (Table 5) are the paper's strongest evidence for DynoNet superiority, but these ratings lack inter-rater reliability metrics, statistical significance testing, and show systematic discrepancies between partner and third-party evaluators.

The ablation study (Table 7) is incomplete: it reports only dev-set loss improvements (0.05–0.10 points) without evaluation on task success metrics or human ratings, making it impossible to assess whether architectural components actually improve dialogue quality.
No statistical significance testing is reported for any performance comparisons (loss, task success, human ratings), undermining confidence in claimed improvements.
Training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset) introduces selection bias that is not analyzed. No comparison of model performance when trained on all vs. successful dialogues only.
Entity linking accuracy is not evaluated, creating an unquantified potential bottleneck in the pipeline.

The dual evaluation framework (partner + third-party) is methodologically innovative and reveals that different evaluation modes measure different aspects of dialogue quality, but the discrepancy analysis is qualitative without quantitative correlation analysis.
Only one domain (MutualFriends) is evaluated; generalization to other collaborative tasks is unclear, undermining claims about the task's broad applicability.
The architectural novelty is incremental: DynoNet extends EntNet by adding message passing over knowledge graph structure, but improvements are modest and not validated on task-level metrics.
disagreements: Reviewers differ on the severity of the task success underperformance: structure_analyst and methodology_auditor flag this as a major flaw requiring claim revision; novelty_assessor_disruptive treats it as a critical contradiction but acknowledges the dataset and problem formulation as strong contributions; claim_verifier emphasizes this as a fundamental inconsistency that undermines the main claims.

Interpretation of human-likeness ratings: methodology_auditor and claim_verifier emphasize the lack of statistical validation and inter-rater reliability; novelty_assessor_incremental acknowledges the ratings but notes they are subjective; novelty_assessor_disruptive treats them as the paper's strongest evidence for DynoNet superiority despite methodological concerns.

Assessment of architectural novelty: novelty_assessor_incremental rates it as low-to-moderate (incremental over EntNet); novelty_assessor_disruptive rates it as moderate novelty (natural extension of existing techniques); claim_verifier emphasizes the incremental nature and modest empirical improvements.

Importance of cross-domain evaluation: structure_analyst and methodology_auditor flag single-domain evaluation as a moderate concern; novelty_assessor_disruptive treats it as a major limitation undermining generalization claims; claim_verifier emphasizes this as a significant gap.

Interpretation of time pressure effects: methodology_auditor and claim_verifier treat 5-minute time constraint as a potential artifact; novelty_assessor_disruptive suggests time pressure may reflect realistic communication constraints; structure_analyst notes this as an unanalyzed confound.

Significance of dataset contribution: all reviewers recognize the dataset as valuable, but structure_analyst and novelty_assessor_disruptive emphasize it as the paper's primary contribution; methodology_auditor and claim_verifier treat it as substantial but limited by single-domain focus.
uncertainty_hotspots: Task success metric interpretation: Is the underperformance of DynoNet relative to Rule baseline a fundamental flaw in the architecture, or does it reflect a deliberate trade-off between task effectiveness and human-likeness? The paper does not explicitly address this.

Human-likeness rating reliability: Without inter-rater reliability metrics, it is unclear whether human-likeness ratings reflect genuine differences in dialogue quality or evaluator disagreement. The discrepancy between partner and third-party evaluators (lines 668–698) suggests they measure different constructs, but this is not quantified.
Loss as proxy for dialogue quality: No correlation analysis between test loss and task success or human ratings. Unclear whether loss improvements translate to practical benefits.
Entity linking accuracy: Unquantified potential bottleneck. Rule-based lexicon (Appendix D) may limit model performance more than architectural design.
Training data selection bias: Impact of training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset) is unknown. No comparison to training on all dialogues.
Generalization beyond MutualFriends: Single-domain evaluation limits confidence in claims about task's broad applicability. Unclear whether findings generalize to other collaborative tasks.
Strategy learning causality: Table 4 shows DynoNet matches human strategic behavior, but no causal analysis. Could be artifact of data distribution rather than learned behavior.
Utterance-level likelihood maximization sufficiency: Foundational assumption unvalidated. No comparison to task-level reward signals (e.g., reinforcement learning).
Time pressure effects: 5-minute constraint may introduce artifacts or reflect realistic communication constraints. No analysis of impact on dialogue naturalness.
Copying mechanism correctness: Example (Table 6) shows DynoNet 'lying' (claiming false information). Unclear if this reflects copying mechanism failure or model generation errors.
model_diversity_effects: Structure_analyst (logical-coherence-first) identifies the contradiction between task success metrics and outperformance claim as a critical logical inconsistency, emphasizing argument chain coherence over empirical details.

Methodology_auditor (reproducibility-and-validity-first) emphasizes missing statistical significance testing, incomplete ablation studies, and unvalidated assumptions as fundamental methodological concerns affecting reproducibility.

Novelty_assessor_incremental (incremental-contribution lens) treats the work as a meaningful but incremental contribution, emphasizing that architectural novelty is limited and problem formulation is the primary novel aspect.

Novelty_assessor_disruptive (disruptive-thinking lens) protects the problem formulation as genuinely novel and underexplored, treating sparse precedent as an innovation signal rather than a weakness, while still flagging empirical inconsistencies.

Claim_verifier (evidence-and-uncertainty-first) systematically evaluates each claim against evidence, identifying the task success contradiction as a factual inconsistency rather than a matter of interpretation.

Role-specific effects: Structure_analyst focuses on logical argument coherence; methodology_auditor emphasizes experimental rigor and reproducibility; novelty assessors differ in how they weight problem formulation vs. architectural innovation; claim_verifier prioritizes evidence-claim alignment.
meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a hybrid contribution with genuine strengths (novel problem formulation, substantial dataset, methodologically innovative dual evaluation) but significant weaknesses in empirical validation and claim-evidence alignment. The primary issue is a direct contradiction between the main claim (DynoNet outperforms baselines) and task success metrics (Rule > DynoNet). This is not a matter of interpretation but a factual inconsistency that must be addressed. Recommend: (1) Revise claims to accurately reflect empirical results (e.g., 'DynoNet achieves higher human-likeness ratings but comparable or lower task success rates compared to Rule baseline'); (2) Provide statistical significance testing for all performance comparisons; (3) Extend ablation study to include task success and human evaluation metrics; (4) Evaluate on at least one additional domain to support generalization claims; (5) Analyze entity linking accuracy and its impact on model performance; (6) Report inter-rater reliability metrics for human evaluation. The dataset and problem formulation are valuable contributions that warrant publication, but the architectural claims require stronger empirical support. Consider whether the paper's primary contribution is the task setting and dataset (strong) or the neural architecture (weak), and position accordingly.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes meaningful contributions to dialogue research through problem formulation and dataset creation. However, several critical issues require attention: (1) The main claim that DynoNet 'outperforms baselines' is contradicted by task success metrics (Table 4). You must either revise this claim or provide analysis explaining why human-likeness ratings are more important than task success. (2) Human-likeness ratings lack statistical validation. Report inter-rater reliability metrics (Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa) and conduct significance testing. (3) The ablation study is incomplete—it uses only dev-set loss. Extend it to include task success and human evaluation metrics to assess whether architectural components are truly 'critical.' (4) Consider the impact of training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset). Compare to training on all dialogues to assess selection bias. (5) Evaluate entity linking accuracy to rule out this as a bottleneck. (6) Evaluate on at least one additional domain to support generalization claims. (7) Analyze the 5-minute time pressure and its effects on dialogue naturalness. These revisions will strengthen the empirical validation and clarify the paper's contributions. The dataset and dual evaluation framework are valuable; focus on making the architectural claims more rigorous.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes a symmetric collaborative dialogue task where two agents with private knowledge communicate to identify a shared item. It contributes: (1) a novel problem formulation bridging task-oriented and open-domain dialogue, (2) an 11K-dialogue human-human corpus (MutualFriends domain) with documented linguistic phenomena, (3) DynoNet, a neural architecture combining knowledge graphs with recurrent embeddings, and (4) a dual evaluation methodology (partner + third-party). The work makes meaningful contributions to problem formulation and dataset creation, which are recognized across all specialist reviews. However, critical inconsistencies emerge between claims and empirical evidence. The primary claim that DynoNet 'outperforms baselines' is directly contradicted by task success metrics (Table 4: DynoNet 0.80 vs Rule 0.82 per turn; 0.89 vs 0.91 per selection). The paper's strongest evidence for DynoNet superiority comes from human-likeness ratings, which are subjective, show systematic discrepancies between evaluation modes, and lack inter-rater reliability reporting. Architectural components (message passing, entity abstraction) show modest improvements on dev-set loss (0.05–0.10 points) without task-level validation. Key methodological concerns include: (1) training only on successful dialogues (79% of data) introduces unanalyzed selection bias; (2) entity linking accuracy not evaluated, creating an unquantified bottleneck; (3) no statistical significance testing for any performance comparisons; (4) crowdsourcing under 5-minute time pressure may not reflect natural dialogue; (5) only one domain evaluated, limiting generalization claims. The dual evaluation framework is methodologically innovative and reveals important insights about evaluation divergence. Overall, the paper's greatest strength is problem formulation and dataset contribution; its greatest weakness is the gap between architectural claims and empirical performance, combined with incomplete methodological validation.
strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: Symmetric collaborative dialogue occupies a conceptually underexplored space between task-oriented and open-domain dialogue. The motivation is clear (conversational implicature, diverse semantics) and the task is well-defined.

Substantial dataset contribution: 11K human-human dialogues collected efficiently (13.5 hours on AMT) with documented linguistic phenomena (coreference, cross-talk, external knowledge use, strategic behavior). Dataset is publicly available and exhibits genuine linguistic complexity.

Methodologically innovative dual evaluation framework: Comparison of partner evaluation (interactive) and third-party evaluation (external observer) reveals that different evaluation modes measure different aspects of dialogue quality. Discrepancy analysis (lines 668–698) provides valuable insights.

Comprehensive documentation of linguistic and pragmatic phenomena: Table 2 systematically categorizes linguistic phenomena with quantified frequencies. Section 2.3 documents strategic behavior (entity/attribute ordering) with clear intuition.

Coherent neural architecture design: DynoNet's combination of knowledge graphs (structured) with recurrent embeddings (unstructured) is well-motivated. Entity abstraction approach (no lookup-table embeddings) is principled. Architecture is clearly presented with helpful visualizations.

Multi-faceted evaluation methodology: Paper reports automatic metrics (loss, utterance length, entropy, utterance types), task success metrics (CT, CS), strategic behavior metrics (#Ent1, |Attr1|), and human evaluation (partner and third-party). This comprehensive approach provides multiple perspectives on model performance.

Honest reporting of limitations: Paper acknowledges that DynoNet underperforms Rule on task success metrics (Table 4) and reports an example where DynoNet 'lies' (Table 6). Discussion of evaluation discrepancies (lines 668–698) is candid about measurement challenges.
limitations: Critical contradiction between main claim and empirical evidence: The paper claims DynoNet 'outperforms baselines in task success' (abstract, lines 198–199), but Table 4 shows DynoNet underperforms Rule baseline on primary task success metrics (CT: 0.80 vs 0.82 per turn; CS: 0.89 vs 0.91 per selection). This is a direct factual inconsistency that undermines the main architectural claim. The paper emphasizes human-likeness ratings instead, which are subjective and lack statistical validation.

No statistical significance testing for any performance comparisons: The paper reports point estimates for loss, task success rates, and human ratings without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Differences of 0.02 in task success rate or 0.3–0.5 points on 5-point rating scales may not be statistically meaningful. This is a fundamental methodological gap affecting all empirical claims.

Ablation study incomplete and limited to dev-set loss only: Table 7 reports ablation results using only dev-set cross-entropy loss. No evaluation of message passing depth (K) or entity abstraction on task success rate (CT, CS) or human evaluation ratings is provided. Loss improvements are modest (0.05–0.10 points) and lack significance testing. Impossible to assess whether architectural components actually improve dialogue quality or task performance.

Training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset) introduces unanalyzed selection bias: Section 4.1 states 'only train on successful dialogues', excluding 21% of data (2,398 failed dialogues). No analysis of failed dialogues or their characteristics. No comparison of model performance when trained on all vs. successful dialogues only. This selection bias may affect generalization and error recovery.

Entity linking accuracy not evaluated; potential bottleneck unquantified: Section 3.1 mentions 'rule-based lexicon to link text spans to entities' (Appendix D) but provides no evaluation of entity linking accuracy. Errors in entity linking could corrupt node embeddings and dialogue state representation. Example (Table 6) shows DynoNet 'lying' (claiming false information); unclear if this reflects entity linking errors or model generation errors.

Only one domain (MutualFriends) evaluated; generalization claims unsupported: All experiments evaluate only on MutualFriends domain. No cross-domain validation provided. Claims about task's broad applicability (Introduction, lines 020–025) and positioning as 'stepping stone towards learning more complex dialogues such as negotiation' (Discussion, lines 725–750) lack empirical support.
open_questions: Why does DynoNet underperform Rule baseline on task success metrics (0.80 vs 0.82 per turn) despite being rated as more human-like? Is this a deliberate trade-off between task effectiveness and naturalness, or does it indicate architectural limitations? How should this trade-off be interpreted in the context of the paper's claims?

What is the inter-rater reliability for human-likeness ratings (Table 5)? Partner and third-party evaluators show systematic discrepancies (lines 668–698), suggesting they measure different constructs. Can you provide Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa for each rating dimension? Are the differences between models statistically significant?

How does entity linking accuracy affect downstream model performance? What is the precision, recall, and F1 score of the rule-based lexicon (Appendix D)? How frequently does entity linking fail, and what is the impact on task success and human evaluation?

What is the impact of training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset)? How do models trained on all dialogues (including failed ones) compare to models trained on successful dialogues only? What are the characteristics of failed dialogues, and why do they fail?

Does DynoNet generalize to other collaborative dialogue tasks beyond MutualFriends? Can you evaluate on at least one additional domain (e.g., negotiation, collaborative planning, product recommendation) to assess generalization of the task setting and architectural approach?

How does the 5-minute time pressure affect dialogue quality and naturalness? Are dialogues collected under time pressure representative of natural human communication? How do linguistic characteristics (utterance length, vocabulary diversity, dialogue acts) compare to other dialogue corpora?

Is utterance-level likelihood maximization sufficient for task-oriented dialogue? How does performance compare to task-level reward signals (e.g., reinforcement learning with task success as reward)? Does task-level training improve task success without sacrificing human-likeness?

What is the correlation between test loss and task success rate? Is cross-entropy loss a valid proxy for dialogue quality in this setting? How do loss improvements translate to practical improvements in task effectiveness or human satisfaction?

transparency_notes: This meta-review synthesizes five specialist reviews with different cognitive roles and epistemic stances. All reviewers identify the same critical contradiction (task success metrics contradict outperformance claim), but differ in how they weight this against other contributions.

The creativity safeguard is applied consistently: sparse precedent for the symmetric collaborative dialogue task is treated as an innovation signal rather than a weakness, protecting the problem formulation from being penalized for divergence from mainstream literature.
Reviewers consistently identify unvalidated foundational assumptions (A1–A10 from shared analysis) as sources of uncertainty. These assumptions are not disputed but their validity is questioned.

No reviewer disputes the factual accuracy of reported metrics. Disagreements concern interpretation (e.g., whether task success underperformance is a flaw or trade-off) and significance (e.g., whether modest loss improvements are practically meaningful).

The paper's transparency about limitations (acknowledging DynoNet underperformance on task success, reporting example of 'lying', discussing evaluation discrepancies) is noted positively by all reviewers, but does not offset the contradiction between claims and evidence.

Reviewers' confidence is constrained by incomplete methodological reporting: missing statistical significance tests, inter-rater reliability metrics, sample sizes, and correlation analyses limit the ability to assess practical significance of reported differences.

The dual evaluation framework is recognized as methodologically valuable, but the discrepancy analysis is noted as qualitative without quantitative validation. This limits the ability to assess which evaluation mode is more predictive of downstream performance.

All reviewers note that the paper's primary contributions are problem formulation and dataset creation, not the neural architecture. However, the paper's framing emphasizes architectural superiority, creating a mismatch between claimed and actual contributions.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a hybrid contribution with genuine strengths (novel problem formulation, substantial dataset, methodologically innovative dual evaluation) but significant weaknesses in empirical validation and claim-evidence alignment. The critical issue is a direct contradiction between the main claim (DynoNet outperforms baselines) and task success metrics (Rule > DynoNet). This must be addressed. Recommended actions: (1) Revise abstract and main claims to accurately reflect empirical results. Either acknowledge that DynoNet underperforms Rule on task success but excels on human-likeness ratings, or provide analysis explaining why human-likeness is the primary metric of interest. (2) Conduct statistical significance testing for all performance comparisons (loss, task success, human ratings). Report p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes. (3) Extend ablation study to include task success metrics (CT, CS) and human evaluation ratings for each ablated model. Assess which components contribute to which aspects of performance. (4) Evaluate on at least one additional domain to support generalization claims. If cross-domain evaluation is not feasible, clearly state limitations. (5) Analyze entity linking accuracy and its impact on model performance. (6) Report inter-rater reliability metrics (Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa) for human evaluation. (7) Analyze characteristics of failed dialogues (21% of dataset) and compare model performance when trained on all vs. successful dialogues only. The dataset and problem formulation are valuable contributions that warrant publication. However, the architectural claims require stronger empirical support. Consider repositioning the paper to emphasize the task setting and dataset as primary contributions, with the neural architecture as a proof-of-concept rather than a major innovation.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes meaningful contributions to dialogue research through problem formulation and dataset creation. However, several critical issues require attention before publication: (1) The main claim that DynoNet 'outperforms baselines in task success' is contradicted by Table 4 (Rule 0.82 > DynoNet 0.80 per turn). You must revise this claim. Either acknowledge that DynoNet underperforms Rule on task success but achieves higher human-likeness ratings, or provide analysis explaining why human-likeness is more important than task success. (2) Human-likeness ratings lack statistical validation. Report inter-rater reliability metrics (Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa) for each rating dimension. Conduct significance testing (e.g., t-tests) for rating differences. Provide sample sizes and confidence intervals. (3) The ablation study is incomplete. Extend Table 7 to include task success metrics (CT, CS) and human evaluation ratings for K ∈ {0,1,2} and entity abstraction variants. This will clarify whether architectural components are truly 'critical'. (4) Analyze the impact of training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset). Compare model performance when trained on all vs. successful dialogues only. Discuss selection bias implications. (5) Evaluate entity linking accuracy on a sample of test dialogues. Report precision, recall, F1. Analyze error propagation and impact on task success. (6) Evaluate on at least one additional domain (e.g., negotiation, collaborative planning) to support generalization claims. If not feasible, clearly state limitations. (7) Analyze the 5-minute time pressure and its effects on dialogue naturalness. Compare linguistic characteristics to other dialogue corpora. These revisions will strengthen empirical validation and clarify contributions. The dataset and dual evaluation framework are valuable; focus on making architectural claims more rigorous or repositioning them as secondary contributions.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes a symmetric collaborative dialogue task where two agents with private knowledge communicate to identify a shared item. It contributes: (1) a novel problem formulation bridging task-oriented and open-domain dialogue, (2) an 11K-dialogue corpus with documented linguistic phenomena, (3) DynoNet (a neural architecture combining knowledge graphs with recurrent embeddings), and (4) a dual evaluation methodology (partner + third-party). The work makes meaningful contributions to problem formulation and dataset creation, but faces critical inconsistencies between claims and empirical evidence.

Strengths:
- Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: Symmetric collaborative dialogue occupies a conceptually underexplored space between task-oriented and open-domain dialogue. The motivation is clear (conversational implicature, diverse semantics) and the task is well-defined.
- Substantial dataset contribution: 11K human-human dialogues collected efficiently (13.5 hours on AMT) with documented linguistic phenomena (coreference, cross-talk, external knowledge use, strategic behavior). Dataset is publicly available and exhibits genuine linguistic complexity.
- Methodologically innovative dual evaluation framework: Comparison of partner evaluation (interactive) and third-party evaluation (external observer) reveals that different evaluation modes measure different aspects of dialogue quality. Discrepancy analysis (lines 668–698) provides valuable insights.
- Comprehensive documentation of linguistic and pragmatic phenomena: Table 2 systematically categorizes linguistic phenomena with quantified frequencies. Section 2.3 documents strategic behavior (entity/attribute ordering) with clear intuition.
- Coherent neural architecture design: DynoNet's combination of knowledge graphs (structured) with recurrent embeddings (unstructured) is well-motivated. Entity abstraction approach (no lookup-table embeddings) is principled. Architecture is clearly presented with helpful visualizations.

Limitations:
- Critical contradiction between main claim and empirical evidence: The paper claims DynoNet 'outperforms baselines in task success' (abstract, lines 198–199), but Table 4 shows DynoNet underperforms Rule baseline on primary task success metrics (CT: 0.80 vs 0.82 per turn; CS: 0.89 vs 0.91 per selection). This is a direct factual inconsistency that undermines the main architectural claim. The paper emphasizes human-likeness ratings instead, which are subjective and lack statistical validation.
- No statistical significance testing for any performance comparisons: The paper reports point estimates for loss, task success rates, and human ratings without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Differences of 0.02 in task success rate or 0.3–0.5 points on 5-point rating scales may not be statistically meaningful. This is a fundamental methodological gap affecting all empirical claims.

Open Questions:
- Why does DynoNet underperform Rule baseline on task success metrics (0.80 vs 0.82 per turn) despite being rated as more human-like? Is this a deliberate trade-off between task effectiveness and naturalness, or does it indicate architectural limitations?
- What is the inter-rater reliability for human-likeness ratings (Table 5)? Partner and third-party evaluators show systematic discrepancies (lines 668–698), suggesting they measure different constructs. Can you provide Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa for each rating dimension?
- How does entity linking accuracy affect downstream model performance? What is the precision, recall, and F1 score of the rule-based lexicon (Appendix D)? How frequently does entity linking fail, and what is the impact on task success and human evaluation?
- What is the impact of training only on successful dialogues (79% of dataset)? How do models trained on all dialogues (including failed ones) compare to models trained on successful dialogues only?

Transparency:
- This meta-review synthesizes five specialist reviews with different cognitive roles and epistemic stances. All reviewers identify the same critical contradiction (task success metrics contradict outperformance claim), but differ in how they weight this against other contributions.
- The creativity safeguard is applied consistently: sparse precedent for the symmetric collaborative dialogue task is treated as an innovation signal rather than a weakness, protecting the problem formulation from being penalized for divergence from mainstream literature.
- Reviewers consistently identify unvalidated foundational assumptions (A1–A10 from shared analysis) as sources of uncertainty. These assumptions are not disputed but their validity is questioned.
- No reviewer disputes the factual accuracy of reported metrics. Disagreements concern interpretation (e.g., whether task success underperformance is a flaw or trade-off) and significance (e.g., whether modest loss improvements are practically meaningful).
- Reviewers' confidence is constrained by incomplete methodological reporting: missing statistical significance tests, inter-rater reliability metrics, sample sizes, and correlation analyses limit the ability to assess practical significance of reported differences.

top_documents.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: recent work in which the distributed representation is driven by supervi- sion from discourse annotations. For example, Ji and Eisenstein (2014) show that RST parsing can be performed by learning task-speciﬁc word repre- sentations, which perform considerably better than generic word2vec representations (Mikolov et al., 2013). Li et al. (2014) propose a recursive neural network approach to RST parsing, which is sim- ilar to the upward pass in our model, and Kalch- brenner and Blunsom (2013) show how a recurrent neural network can be used to identify dialogue acts. However, prior work has not applied these ideas to the classiﬁcation of implicit relations in the PDTB, and does not consider the role of en- tities. As we argue in the introduction, a single vector representation is insufﬁciently expressive, because it obliterates the entity chains that help to tie discourse together. More generally, our entity-augmented dis- tributed representation can be viewed in the con- text of recent literature on combining distributed and formal semantics: by representing entities, we are taking a small step away from purely vectorial representations, and towards more tra- ditional logical representations of meaning. In this sense, our approach is “bottom-up”, as we try to add a small amount of logical formalism to distributed representations; other approaches are “top-down”, softening purely logical repre- sentations by using distributional clustering

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: - logue data are available, simply training on human- human dialogue is seldom directly useful. System behavior changes affect user behavior, which affects the system’s next actions, so any improvement to the system can have unpredictable consequences. In short, learning interactive behaviors is fundamental- ly different from learning input-output mappings, and is likely to require new approaches. In summary, this section has argued that dialogue involves many challenges for learning, and that addressing them will require new methods that: make fewer assumptions, require less data, can mod - el the details of human cognitive processing, and can operate across multiple levels. Challenge F: Compositional Policy Specification Today dialogue systems are hard to port to new domains. This is especially true for interactive behav - iors: today typically tied to specific decision points, current “nodules of interactivity” are limited in applicability to the exact context in which they appear. We would instead like to build interactive sys - tems from more general conversational skills, as reusable components. For example, imagining that we have developed a general policy for choosing the next interview question, a general policy for showing empathy, and a general policy for supportive turn taking, we could imagine that these could be com - posed to produce a system capable of effective, natu - ral, and warm first-encounter dialogues.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

For example, Ji and Eisenstein (2014) show that RST parsing can be performed by learning task-speciﬁc word repre- sentations, which perform considerably better than generic word2vec representations (Mikolov et al., 2013). Li et al. (2014) propose a recursive neural network approach to RST parsing, which is sim- ilar to the upward pass in our model, and Kalch- brenner and Blunsom (2013) show how a recurrent neural network can be used to identify dialogue acts. However, prior work has not applied these ideas to the classiﬁcation of implicit relations in the PDTB, and does not consider the role of en- tities. As we argue in the introduction, a single vector representation is insufﬁciently expressive, because it obliterates the entity chains that help to tie discourse together. More generally, our entity-augmented dis- tributed representation can be viewed in the con- text of recent literature on combining distributed and formal semantics: by representing entities, we are taking a small step away from purely vectorial representations, and towards more tra- ditional logical representations of meaning. In this sense, our approach is “bottom-up”, as we try to add a small amount of logical formalism to distributed representations; other approaches are “top-down”, softening purely logical repre- sentations by using distributional clustering

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: - logue data are available, simply training on human- human dialogue is seldom directly useful. System behavior changes affect user behavior, which affects the system’s next actions, so any improvement to the system can have unpredictable consequences. In short, learning interactive behaviors is fundamental- ly different from learning input-output mappings, and is likely to require new approaches. In summary, this section has argued that dialogue involves many challenges for learning, and that addressing them will require new methods that: make fewer assumptions, require less data, can mod - el the details of human cognitive processing, and can operate across multiple levels. Challenge F: Compositional Policy Specification Today dialogue systems are hard to port to new domains. This is especially true for interactive behav - iors: today typically tied to specific decision points, current “nodules of interactivity” are limited in applicability to the exact context in which they appear. We would instead like to build interactive sys - tems from more general conversational skills, as reusable components. For example, imagining that we have developed a general policy for choosing the next interview question, a general policy for showing empathy, and a general policy for supportive turn taking, we could imagine that these could be com - posed to produce a system capable of effective, natu - ral, and warm first-encounter dialogues.

top_documents.title: Document 2
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections).
